title: Allow per-subproject overrides for how dependencies are installed
description:
Mole auto-runs `npm install --omit=dev` for plain npm groups when `node_modules` is missing, but it can't install everything itself:

- yarn-workspace projects (yarn 1 and yarn 4) must be installed manually first, because npm can't resolve their workspace-linked packages.
- Some npm groups point at vendor working directories that only exist after a project-specific vendoring step.

Today these require out-of-band manual pre-installs, documented per consuming project. It would be nice if a scan group could declare, in `mole.toml`, the command mole should run to materialize its dependency tree (e.g. `install_cmd = "yarn install"`), so the tool can prepare each subproject the right way instead of relying on the operator to do it by hand.

title: Multi-version packages spanning NOTICE/NOTICE-SUPPLEMENT are over-disclosed in each document's body
description:
When the same package appears at different versions in scan groups that land in separate output documents (e.g. `postcss` 8.5.15 in one group and 8.5.3 in another), the version-grouping logic causes *each* document to also emit the *other* document's version section in its component-licenses body (and the primary document's package list may show both versions).

Every version is still fully listed and disclosed in its proper document, so this is harmless over-disclosure rather than a missing-disclosure bug — but automated license reviewers flag the body/index mismatch, and it produces confusing diffs.

The fix likely belongs in the exclude/version-group rendering (`src/license_mole/render/__init__.py`) so that a document only emits the version sections that belong to it.

title: Define license rendering in mole.toml
description:
### Problem statement

Currently, license identifiers are translated to short and long names in `render/labels.py`. An identifier that doesn't appear in these tables is rendered as-is in the output for both short and long names and uses the default text to render the licensing message.

This doesn't scale well, as it requires submitting a change to Mole whenever a project has a new license.

To make this more practical, Mole should support extending these tables at runtime using configuration options specified in `mole.toml`.

### Suggested syntax

CC0 is already supported by Mole, but since it uses a custom license message that may need to be reformatted in some documents it serves as a good example:

```toml
[license."CC0-1.0"]
short = "CC0"
long = "CC0 1.0 Universal"
message = "Released using CC0"  # optional
```

### Suggested implementation

It should work to modify the dicts in `render.labels` from inside `config.load_config()`. If a license already exists, the text should be overridden.

In the tradition of Postel's Law, there should be no need to perform explicit validation of the configuration except to verify that any values that are set must be strings, as the default behaviors are sensible.

title: Handle license text where a SPDX identifier was expected
description:
## Problem

Projects maintained by the IPython team include license information in `pyproject.toml` that looks like this:
```toml
license = {file = "LICENSE"}
```
(Example: https://github.com/ipython/ipykernel/blob/main/pyproject.toml#L9)

It would be possible for Mole to deal with this syntax if it were parsing the `pyproject.toml` files directly, but when fetching metadata from PyPI, it has already been preprocessed. This results in the entire contents of the license file being presented in the `license` property.

The freeform nature of the license field in NPM `package.json` files also allows similarly unexpected contents to be inserted into the license field. For example, the `@github/copilot-language-server` package used to have a URL there instead of a SPDX-style identifier.

Presuming that the unexpected syntax didn't trigger an exception earlier in the process, the end result is a very noisy set of error messages at the end of validation that requires manual intervention to address.

## Workarounds

For the most part, this can be addressed by the user through overrides. 

However, this is a predictable issue resulting from sensible project configurations, so this is being classified as a bug instead of an enhancement.

## Possible Solutions

* License strings that are excessively long or that contain too many tokens could be ignored.
    * This could have false negatives: a short line of freeform text could still yield an invalid identifier.
    * If this is sufficiently uncommon, then overrides become an acceptable solution.
* Certain keywords (such as `Copyright`) could be a signal that it is license text instead of a license identifier.
    * Since the formatting will have been lost, it is probably not desirable to guess at the license identifier and it definitely can't be used as license text, so it probably will need to be ignored.
* The license string could be ignored if there are too many unknown license types.

title: Links are incorrectly generated
description:
We found five problems when generating links. These issues aren't really related to each other, but this issue will track them together.

### Nested hyperlinks

Under some circumstances that have yet to be determined, the Markdown generator doesn't detect that a URL is already contained within a Markdown hyperlink, leading to a pattern like `[text]([url](url))` or `[[text](url)](url)` ~~, and in one case `<url>` was rendered as `[url](<url>)`.~~ This case resolved in 0.3.0.

### Inconsistent anchor hashes

~~When packages or versions are merged, some internal links can end up with the wrong anchor.~~ Resolved in 0.2.2.

### Missing `#` in shared license links

~~Internal links to shared license text are missing the leading `#`. (This might possibly be a configuration issue in `mole.toml` -- investigate.)~~ Resolved in 0.2.2.

### "(Could not find homepage for package)"

In `RenderPackage.__init__()`, `HomepageMissingError` is caught and stored in the rendered package's `url` property. This was supposed to be a temporary implementation but since I forgot to put a `TODO:` comment on it, it's still there. This results in bogus URLs in the output.

### Repository-relative links

~~The URLs to vendored packages are intended to point to the appropriate repository instead of upstream. Nothing was ever implemented to resolve these to real links, and they may even include absolute paths for the machine that generated the output.~~

~~Fixing this properly will require the ability to define a link to the project's own repository, which may also require versioning.~~

Mostly resolved in 0.3.0. However, versioned links must be explicitly managed inside `mole.toml`. There is room for future improvement here.

### Common thread: Error detection

None of these would have slipped through the cracks if there was better error detection during the rendering process to ensure that all links are either valid URLs or anchors that were actually generated in the output.

title: New project bootstrapping tool
description:
There is a commented-out `-g` flag for generating an initial `mole.toml` file for a project.

This flag should do the following:

* Prompt the user for basic project information.
* Ask the user if they prefer Markdown output, plain text output, or both.
* Generate a template file based on the answers to the above.
* Find all `package.json`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, and `pyproject.toml` files.
* Find all `.txt` files that contain `dependency()` blocks.
* Find all `requirements.txt` files that don't have corresponding `pyproject.toml` files.
* If #2 is implemented, find any SBOM files that can be used to identify dependencies.
* Generate a `mole.toml` file containing:
    * Minimal configuration for the chosen output format.
    * Groups for all of the detected project files.
    * A single collection containing all of the created groups.

title: License compatibility enforcement
description:
Since not all open-source licenses are mutually compatible and may introduce restrictions that aren't present in a project's own license, it would be useful for Mole to detect incompatible licenses.

It probably isn't reliable to hard-code some sort of compatibility matrix into Mole itself. A better strategy would be to allow the user to specify a list of acceptable licenses in `mole.toml`, and then Mole can throw an error if a dependency has a license that isn't in that list. The user can then choose to add that license to the acceptable list, or they can take whatever steps are necessary to remove that dependency from their project.

This feature should be opt-in. If no list of acceptable licenses is specified, no restrictions should be applied.

### Possible enhancements to consider

* Provide a command-line flag to instruct Mole to update `mole.toml` with the licenses that are currently detected.
* Allow individual packages to be marked as permitted despite having a license that is not otherwise accepted.

### Possible challenges

Since `mole.toml` can reference other TOML files, it might not be immediately obvious which file the command-line flag should update.

title: Baseline documentation
description:
Mole needs documentation, and there's not much here right now.

There are three parts to this task:
1. Flesh out any missing API documentation, including properly documenting instance variables.
2. Write documentation for the `mole.toml` format.
3. Write documentation for the CLI tool and how to integrate it with workflows.

title: Plain-text formatting
description:
### Background

Plain text is currently not much different than Markdown. Right now the plain-text documents are rendered as Markdown with a couple small configuration changes, and then blockquotes are converted into indentation, HTML entities are translated, and links are stripped. Everything else is handled by the configuration. This means that there are still some points that could be improved.

(If this gets too complex, turn this into an epic.)

### Word wrapping

The license files are embedded more-or-less as-is into the output document aside from some fixups and blockquoting. This isn't generally a problem in Markdown, but in plain text an unwrapped input file can look like a mess.

Python's `textwrap` library isn't suitable for this role. It doesn't have paragraph detection and it doesn't understand hanging indents. Some sort of state machine is likely to be a better solution.

### Headings

The Markdown implementation converts underlines into `##` headings. `##` headings don't look terrible in plain text, but a format option to convert them the other direction could be welcome.

### Emphasis

There are a couple of documents that use some emphasis formatting that looks awkward as plain text. Consider some options to clean that up.

title: Epic: Alternatives and optional dependencies
description:
Mole currently skips over optional dependencies and dev dependencies. It typically makes sense to skip these for transitive dependencies, since the main project will explicitly depend on anything it requires that might be optional for one of its dependencies.

However, there are cases where this behavior might not be appropriate. For example, a user may want to generate an additional document that describes a project's own dev dependencies, or the main project may build more than one package with different features enabled.

Additionally, some dependencies may vary based on environment. For example, a Python package may have different dependencies based on the version of Python in use, or a C++ program may link to different libraries on Windows than on macOS.

To support these use cases, these tasks should be considered:

* Support specifying package groups or "extras" for packages listed in `mole.toml`
* Support specifying environment conditions per output
* Support specifying a dependency's environment requirements in overrides
* Support specifying a dependency's environment requirements in manual metadata
* Support querying CMake for dependencies that vary by configuration (see #5)
* Add command-line flags to control conditional rendering

It's not currently clear if all of these tasks are required or even a good idea. More investigation will be necessary.

title: Improve CMake support
description:
Because Mole naively searches CMakeLists.txt files for `dependency()` blocks, it can't resolve CMake variables or conditional logic.

Mole could provide a standardized implementation of `dependency()` as a CMake module. This would allow Mole to query CMake instead of parsing the files directly. Shipping a standardized CMake module would also simplify adoption.

A standalone implementation should be retained for non-CMake projects. However, the current implementation of this parsing only supports a single argument per line, and it requires the package name to be on the same line as the `(` character. These parsing requirements are inconsistent with how CMake parses it, so the parser should be overhauled.

title: Epic: Java support
description:
During pre-open-source development, Mole had some limited support for Java. It was slow, hacky, and probably wrong, so it was removed in favor of expanding the "manual" dependency handling.

This should be reintroduced in the future. These tasks will be necessary:

* Analyze common project file formats to locate sources and dependency pathing
* Inspect .jar files for `METADATA.mf`
* Inspect .jar files for license text
* Use `jdeps` to identify dependencies for post-Java 9 projects
* Identify what packages are used in pre-Java 9 projects
* Use Maven package repository to collect information not present locally

title: Generate SBOMs from dependencies
description: Since Mole is already doing a lot of work to collect dependency information, in addition to a human-readable document it would be useful to be able to generate a machine-readable summary of the dependencies and their versions and licensing in the form of an SBOM.

title: Collect dependencies from SBOMs
description:
There are two commonly used kinds of SBOMs in circulation:

* [SPDX](https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v3.0.1/model/Software/Classes/Sbom/)
* [CycloneDX](https://github.com/CycloneDX/specification)

Consider supporting these formats as sources of dependency metadata to allow Mole to be used to generate documentation for projects that already have good dependency analysis in place. Third-party SBOM generators would also allow Mole to work for other programming languages that aren't directly supported.

title: Epic: Python support
description:
The current Python support is the bare minimum necessary for Mole to analyze itself. Fleshing it out is going to require considering a bunch of things:

* **`packaging`:** It's worth looking into the existing tooling to see if Mole can avoid reinventing some wheels. <sub>(Pun only somewhat intended.)</sub>
* **Project support:** Thanks to `pyproject.toml` being standardized, the current implementation handles most Python projects, but there are a lot out there that still use `requirements.txt`, `requirements.in`, `Pipfile`, `setup.cfg`, or even `setup.py`.
* **Lockfile support:** Some build systems generate `requirements.txt` as a lockfile format. There's also `Pipfile.lock`, PEP 751, and whatever uv/Rye, PDM, pip-tools, Flit, and Hatch use.
* **virtualenv support:** The Go scanner can collect versioning and licensing information from the installed packages. This should be possible for Python.
* **Groups support:** Mole recognizes Poetry groups but only enough to be able to ignore anything but `main`. This works for skipping dev dependencies, but it doesn't work for optional features.
* **Extras support:** I'm not sure how robust the current extras implementation is. It's enough to let Mole scan itself but it hasn't been exercised any farther.
* **Markers support:** The only supported marker right now is `extras`.

Not all of these tasks are of equal priority and some may depend on other effort that has yet to be done.
